beats.text: If a division leaves something over, is the answer finished? Today we are interpreting remainders. We will compare a situation where everyone needs a place with a situation where the leftover amount can be shared. The context decides what the remainder means.
Our learning goal is to interpret remainders to answer real-world division problems.
board: Interpret remainders to answer real-world division problems.

beats.text: Success criteria. I can check that a remainder is smaller than the divisor. I can decide when a whole extra group is needed. I can share a remainder as a fraction when appropriate.
board: 1. Check that a remainder is smaller than the divisor.
2. Decide when a whole extra group is needed.
3. Share a remainder as a fraction when appropriate.

beats.text: A remainder must be smaller than the divisor. Check a division using groups times group size plus the remainder. Then decide whether to round up, keep whole groups, or share the remainder as a fraction. In a small model, seventeen counters make three full groups of five, with two left over.
Sixty-seven students need teams of up to eight. Eight full teams hold sixty-four students, leaving three students.
Everyone needs a team, so one more team is needed. Nine teams have enough places, although the last team is not full. Eight teams would leave three students out.
Share twenty-three litres equally among four containers. Five litres in each container uses twenty litres, leaving three litres.
Share those three litres equally too. Each container gets three quarters of a litre more, so the amount is five and three quarter litres, or five point seven five litres.

A remainder of three does not automatically mean point three. In our litre problem, the three leftover litres are shared between four containers. Each gets three quarters of a litre more. The divisor and the story explain the fractional part.
beats.chapter: A remainder is not automatically a decimal

beats.text: Thirty-one students travel in cars with five student seats each. How many cars are needed?
Six cars hold thirty students, leaving one student. A seventh car is needed, so the contextual answer is seven cars.

Calculate and check the remainder, then return to the story. People need whole places; divisible quantities can be shared further. Explain your answer using the correct unit. Choose a model and explain why your strategy works.
board: A remainder is smaller than the divisor
